text:
Every recursive resolver keeps copies of the answers it receives. Each record has a TTL, a 32-bit counter of seconds defined in RFC 1035, which lets the resolver reuse the answer without asking the authoritative server again.

Suppose you change an A record at noon, and its TTL is 3600 seconds. A resolver that was queried at 11:59 will keep giving out the old IP until nearly 1 p.m. Clients assume the address is current, because nothing tells them otherwise. So the time it takes for resolver caches to expire, not the edit itself, determines how long the change takes to propagate.

Negative answers are cached too. Under RFC 2308, if a resolver cached an NXDOMAIN before your new subdomain existed, it will keep saying the subdomain doesn't exist until the SOA minimum runs out.

Browsers and OS stub resolvers add their own private caches on top, and some of them ignore TTLs entirely.

I call this TTL debt. To avoid it, operators have to plan both ends of a migration. They should lower the TTL to 300 seconds one full old-TTL period before the move. Otherwise, the internet keeps navigating by an outdated map.
